editorial:
J'accuse! (1919) is a French silent epic written and directed by Abel Gance, produced by Charles PathÃ© under the PathÃ© FrÃ¨res banner, and first released in France on April 25, 1919. The film follows poet Jean Diaz and his romantic rival FranÃ§ois as both are conscripted into WWI, culminating in Gance's celebrated 'Return of the Dead' sequence â€” fallen soldiers rise from their graves to judge whether France was worthy of their sacrifice, a scene Gance filmed using actual troops briefly recalled from the Verdun front. The US theatrical release came in 1921 through United Artists, with D.W. Griffith's support. Gance returned to the premise with a sound remake under the same title in 1938.

For a creator, the underlying 1919 print is in the US public domain without ambiguity: the maximum US copyright term for any 1919 publication is 75 years (28-year initial term plus 47-year renewal under the 1976 Act), expiring December 31, 1994. URAA restoration does not revive it â€” the 'remainder' URAA could restore is zero because the entire 75-year ceiling had already run out before URAA's effective date of January 1, 1996. The genuine trap is the 2008 Lobster Films and Flicker Alley restoration, built from the only surviving tinted nitrate copy at the Nederlands Filmmuseum and featuring a new orchestral score by Robert Israel. That restoration and score are separately protected. Virtually every commercially distributed copy â€” the Flicker Alley DVD, the theatrical DCP, and most streaming versions â€” is the Lobster Films restoration, not the raw 1919 print. Before using footage in a project, confirm your source is the unrestored archival material, not a downstream re-encode of the 2008 restoration.
faq: Is the 1919 J'accuse! print free to use in the US?

The 1919 print is in the US public domain â€” the maximum 75-year copyright term (under the 1976 Copyright Act) expired December 31, 1994. However, the 2008 Lobster Films/Flicker Alley restoration with Robert Israel's orchestral score is separately protected. If your source is the Flicker Alley DVD, a theatrical DCP, or most streaming copies, you are working from a protected restoration, not the public domain source material.
Does the French origin of J'accuse! create a URAA copyright problem in the US?

No, not for a 1919 publication. URAA (17 U.S.C. Â§ 104A) restores foreign works only for the 'remainder' of the US copyright term. The maximum US term for a 1919 work was 75 years, expiring December 31, 1994 â€” before URAA's effective date of January 1, 1996. There is no remaining term to restore. URAA raises a genuine issue for foreign works published roughly 1923â€“1977, but not for this film.
